study.title: Psalm 138: praise, faithfulness and trust in God's care
study.overview: Psalm 138 is a song of David that unites gratitude for what God has already done, confidence in what He will do and hope that the Lord's reach exceeds the personal life of the psalmist. The psalm begins with intense and public praise, because God answered and strengthened his servant. Then he magnifies the vision: the kings of the earth will hear and praise the Lord, for the glory of God becomes known by his words and ways. Then the psalmist highlights the greatness of God, who, although exalted, turns to the humble and opposes pride. The closure is of persevering faith: God will complete what has begun, and the goodness of the Lord will not fail.

outline.title: Personal praise for received responses
outline.explanation: David promises to praise with all his heart, with sincerity and zeal. He attributes to God the answer to his cry and inner strengthening, celebrating the divine goodness and faithfulness that sustained his life.

outline.title: The Universal Range of God's Glory
outline.explanation: The testimony of the psalmist expands: the kings of the earth will praise the Lord when they hear his words. Worship ceases to be only personal and become public and universal, linked to the paths and glory of the Lord.

outline.title: God exalts the humble and preserves his work
outline.explanation: The psalm concludes with the tension between the height of God and his attention to the humble. Even in distress, the psalmist trusts that the Lord will quicken him, defend him and complete his work, without abandoning what his hands have begun.

study.context: The given notes treat the psalm as part of a final collection associated with David, with tone of gratitude and confidence. It is not necessary to define with certainty the specific historical occasion. According to commentators, the text may also function as community praise in times of deliverance, but this is an interpretative reading, not an uncontroversial statement of the verse itself.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm affirms that God is worthy of praise because it unites majesty and closeness. He is not only above all; he also responds to the cry, strengthens the faithful and cares for the humble. The truth of God appears in his words and promises, and his faithfulness is celebrated as something that exceeds mere reputation: the Lord confirms who He is through what He does. The psalm also projects a broad hope: the worship of the Lord will reach kings, and by extension the nations. Finally, the final prayer confesses that the life of the believer is in the hands of God, who completes his work without abandoning what began.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm presents the Lord as God of gods, and the praise of the nations and kings is united to the worship of Israel.
David praises God with sincerity and fervour with all my heart, without fear of doing so before great people.
The final trust of the psalmist is that God will complete what is lacking to do and will not abandon the work of his hands.

questions: Is my praise to God born of sincere gratitude or just religious habit?
How does my life make the ways and faithfulness of the Lord visible to others?
Have I trusted that God will complete the work that began in me, or live as if it all depended on me?
study.practice: This week, take time to remember God's concrete answers to his cry and turn it into prayer and praise. Also practice a visible humility: recognize before God an area in which you need it to be strengthened. Finally, give Him a project or a fight in progress, praying with the words of the psalm so that the Lord completes his work without abandoning you.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes do not allow to safely fix a specific historical occasion for the psalm. There is also a difference between commentators on the expression of verse 1 and the exact extension of verse 8, but here they were presented as possible interpretations, not as indisputable conclusions.
